22376-love-to-the-uttermost-expositions-:
Love to the Uttermost gives expositions of John chapters thirteen through twenty-one, dated 1898. Those chapters cover Christ's last night with his disciples and beyond. The commentary begins, though, in the Temple courts of older worship.

Two objects met the entering worshipper there: the Brazen Altar and the Laver. The Laver stood always full of pure, fresh water. Priests washed there before their consecration for holy work. They washed before putting on the robes of sacred office. From such types, the expositions move to Christ's washing of feet. Readers get careful verse-by-verse teaching. It serves study of John's Gospel in a devout, detailed style.
26878-the-repairing-restoration-of-violi:
Horace Petherick wrote this manual of violin repair for The Strad Library. It was published in London by the Strad Office and in New York by Charles Scribner's Sons in 1903, and illustrated by the author himself. Petherick served on the music juries at South Kensington in 1885 and Edinburgh in 1890. He acted as an expert in the law courts in 1891, and was vice-president of the Cremona Society. His book speaks from the bench, not the shelf.

Its chapters move from slight accidents, glue, cramps, and joints through injuries to scroll, peg-box, and neck, grafting, fingerboard work, and the removal of the upper table. Later chapters treat worm-holes, warped tables, old superfluous glue, lost portions, and matching wood grain. The closing advice is practical throughout: parts must fit without the slightest looseness or wriggling before they are glued for good.
30916-a-new-long-eared-myotis-myotis-evo:
Rollin H. Baker and Howard J. Stains wrote this short scientific paper for the University of Kansas Publications, Museum of Natural History, volume nine, number three, pages 81 to 84, dated December 10, 1955. Kansas field parties collected long-eared bats across Coahuila, Nuevo León, and Tamaulipas, and examination placed them in Myotis evotis while matching none of its named subspecies. Baker and Stains therefore name and describe a new one.

The new subspecies is Myotis evotis auriculus, with an adult female skin and skull, number 55110 in the Kansas museum, as its type. She was taken ten miles west and two miles south of Piedra, at twelve hundred feet in the Sierra de Tamaulipas, on June 9, 1953, by Gerd H. Heinrich. Its range runs through coastal foothills and nearby mountains from central Coahuila south and east to central Veracruz, with small ears and dark, tawny upper parts.
32187-pleistocene-soricidae-from-san-jos:
James S. Findley's Pleistocene Soricidae from San Josecito Cave, Nuevo Leon, Mexico, appeared on December 1, 1953. It forms volume five, number thirty-six, pages 633 to 639, of the University of Kansas Publications, Museum of Natural History. Findley reports that bones of a large number of Pleistocene vertebrates were taken from San Josecito Cave near Aramberri, in Nuevo Leon, Mexico. Stock reported them in part in 1942, and Cushing in 1945.

Some of those bones, lent to Kansas University by the California Institute of Technology, hold twenty-six lower jaw halves and one snout of shrew-like insect eaters. Findley notes that Mexico's Ice Age shrews were, as far as known, still unstudied. Readers get a short, technical fossil paper, identifying Ice Age shrews from a Mexican cave, jaw by jaw.
8381-expositions-of-holy-scripture-st-jo:
Alexander MacLaren continues his expositions of John's Gospel here, covering chapters 15 to 21. Contents move from the true vine and abiding in love, through the oneness of the branches and Christ's friends, to the farewell discourses, the arrest, the cross, and the risen Lord's appearances. Each passage becomes a sermon, verse by verse.

MacLaren, Manchester's great Baptist preacher, works textually and pastorally: he opens the words, draws their meaning, and presses them toward daily conduct. Preachers kept his expositions as models of clear, warm preaching, and lay readers still use them as devotional reading. The volume suits anyone reading John slowly, passage by passage.
britannica-1911-biloxi:
Biloxi is a city in Harrison County, Mississippi, on Biloxi Bay at the Gulf of Mexico. It lies 80 miles north-east of New Orleans by rail, and 61 miles south-east of Mobile. The 1911 Britannica entry gives 5,467 people in 1900 and 7,988 in 1910. A Louisville and Nashville branch serves the city. An electric railway runs to Bay St Louis through Gulfport. A fine beach of about twelve miles rings its peninsula.

Biloxi works as both a summer and a winter resort, chiefly for New Orleans and Mobile visitors. Hotels, boarding houses, and sanatoriums line the beach road. Its main industries can oysters, shrimp, fish, figs, and vegetables. Fertilizer and flour making also employ the town. An earlier French settlement in this region, called Old Biloxi, was abandoned in 1702. The present site was settled in 1712, the first permanent settlement in modern Mississippi.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-benedict:
Pope Benedict XI, born Nicholas Boccasini at Treviso in 1240, reigned briefly from October 1303 to July 1304. He entered the Dominicans at fourteen, studied fourteen years, and became lector of theology. In 1296 he was elected Master General of the Order.

As general he forbade his friars to favour opponents of Boniface VIII and ordered them to defend the legitimacy of Boniface's election in sermons. Boniface rewarded that loyalty with embassies, the cardinalate in 1298, and the bishopric of Ostia. In 1303 Boccasini stood by Boniface against Nogaret and Colonna at Anagni. Elected pope on 22 October, he restored peace with France, absolving Philip the Fair and his subjects from Boniface's censures.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-clement-:
Pope Clement XI, born Giovanni Francesco Albani at Urbino on 23 July 1649, was elected on 23 November 1700 and died at Rome on 19 March 1721. Sent to Rome at eleven for the Roman College, he was an author at eighteen, translating Greek into elegant Latin, and joined Queen Christina of Sweden's academy before he came of age. He took doctorates in canon and civil law and rose swiftly: prelate at twenty-eight, governor of Rieti, Sabina, and Orvieto, then Secretary of Papal Briefs for thirteen years.

Made cardinal in 1690 and ordained priest, he was chosen after a forty-six-day conclave blocked France's veto of Mariscotti. The Sacred College picked the fifty-one-year-old Albani for virtue and ability, spending three days overcoming his reluctance. His reign opened as Charles II of Spain died childless, leaving his empire to French and Austrian ambition over Philip of Anjou's contested inheritance.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-gregory-:
Pope Gregory XI, born Pierre Roger de Beaufort in 1331 at Maumont in Limoges, was elected at Avignon in December 1370 and died at Rome on 27 March 1378. Nephew of Clement VI, he was heaped with benefices and made cardinal-deacon at eighteen in 1348. He studied at Perugia and became a skilled canonist and theologian. He won esteem for humility and purity of heart.

After Urban V's death the cardinals unanimously elected him. He was ordained priest on 4 January 1371 and crowned the next day. He failed to reconcile France and England but pacified Castile, Aragon, Navarre, Sicily, and Naples. He pursued Greek reunion, crusade, and clerical reform. Soon Italy consumed him: Bernabò Visconti of Milan seized papal fiefs and forced legates to eat their excommunication bull. That drove Gregory to war in 1372, until imperial, Neapolitan, Hungarian, and Hawkwood's support brought a truce in June 1374.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-innocent:
Pope Innocent XI, Benedetto Odescalchi, born at Como 16 May 1611, died at Rome 11 August 1689. Jesuits schooled him at Como, and he read law at Rome and Naples. Urban VIII piled offices on him: prothonotary, head of the Apostolic Camera, Ancona's commissary, Macerata's administrator, and Picena's governor. The next pope, Innocent X, gave him the deacon's title of Santi Cosma e Damiano, and later the priest's title of Sant'Onofrio; the first dignity came in 1645.

Fellow cardinals loved him for deep piety, charity, and selfless devotion to duty. As legate to famine-hit Ferrara, the pope presented him as the poor's father. Novara's bishopric came to him in 1650, and he poured all its revenues into the poor and sick. With papal leave he handed Novara to his brother Giulio in 1656 and moved to Rome. After two months without a pope he won unanimous election 21 September 1676.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-john-xi:
Pope John XI, birth date unknown, rose in 931 and died in 936. Marozia bore him by Alberic. Some writers, following Liutprand and the Liber Pontificalis, call him Sergius III's natural son. His mother then ruled Rome, and her schemes lifted him to Peter's Chair, where Rome's Senatrix et Patricia held sway over him.

To firm her grip Marozia wed Hugh, her brother-in-law, King of Provence and Italy, whose harsh rule in Rome stirred the nobles into opposition behind Alberic II, her younger son. That party toppled Marozia and Hugh; she went to prison, he got away. Alberic took Rome's reins, and the pope, hurt by his mother's downfall, fell largely under his brother, keeping only spiritual duties. Every other jurisdiction, secular, ran through Alberic.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-leo-xi:
Alessandro Ottaviano de' Medici was born at Florence in 1535. He was kin to Leo X through his mother. He longed for the priesthood from boyhood. He waited for his mother's death to be ordained. He served fifteen years as Tuscan envoy to Pius V. He became bishop of Pistoia, then archbishop of Florence, then cardinal. As legate to France he curbed Huguenot sway at Henry IV's court.

He was chosen pope on 1 April 1605 at seventy. French backing shaped the conclave against Spain's wishes. He fell ill at once. He died twenty-seven days later. The entry stresses his refusal to practise nepotism. He even dismissed a confessor who pressed him to make a grandnephew cardinal.

expositions-of-holy-scripture-st-john-ch:
Maclaren's Expositions volume on St. John chapters XV to XXI covers Christ's farewell teaching and passion. Alexander Maclaren expounds short texts in sermon order. The True Vine opens the volume from John XV. Abiding in Love and Christ's Friends follow from the same chapter.

John XVI brings The Guide into All Truth and Sorrow Turned into Joy. Peace and Victory closes that chapter's run. John XVII is treated as The Intercessor and The High Priest's Prayer. The Folded Flock and Christ's Summary of His Work end the prayer section. Later entries move to Christ before Caiaphas and the trial scenes. Maclaren dwells on comfort, prayer, and abiding union in these sermons.
podcast-joerogan-XN-sk8dE9xI:
A statue that holds a mummified monk inside it is the subject of a segment of the Joe Rogan Experience. Scans of an ancient Chinese Buddha statue revealed a seated human skeleton within, a monk who may have mummified himself through a grim ritual years long.

Rogan works through the discovery and the practice behind it, in which monks slowly starved and preserved their own bodies as acts of devotion. The talk asks what such faith asks of a person. The segment is a short, eerie piece of religious history, the kind of true oddity the show loves to pass along.
podcast-tuckercarlson-REEtJTqJbxI:
Journalist Matt Taibbi joins Tucker Carlson to discuss the secret files President Trump has been releasing. Taibbi, famous for his work on the Twitter Files, champions full declassification of government records. Here he argues for what should come out next.

Taibbi lists the files he most wants opened, from assassination records to intelligence abuses. He explains how secrecy protects officials more than it protects the country. Carlson asks whether Trump will really follow through against agency resistance. Curious viewers get a reporter's map of the vaults and a case for throwing them open.
un-ga-res-2200-xxi:
Adopted on December 16, 1966, General Assembly Resolution 2200 (XXI) gave the world its two great human rights covenants. The Roman numeral marks the Assembly's twenty-first session. Catalog copies that date it to 1948 are wrong; 1948 brought the Universal Declaration, while the binding treaties came eighteen years later.

One covenant guards civil and political rights, such as free speech and fair trials. The other covers work, health, schooling, and a fair standard of living. A third short text let people appeal to a UN body about abuses. States then signed and ratified the pair over the next decade, and they still anchor rights law today.
